figures.caption: Figure 2: Framework overview. A context operator τ exposes EEG structure and converts each labeled support trial into one or more instances. The frozen predictor ficl conditions on these instances to predict the query; multi-instance outputs are aggregated to the trial level, and an optional post-hoc calibration stage can adjust the operating point. No parameter of ficl is updated for the target dataset.

Figure 3: EEG context construction. The operator τ = τinfer ◦ τfeat ◦ τinfo combines exactly one feature type with optional temporal/spatial structure and inference-time strategies. One trial can remain one context instance or expand into local views whose predictions are aggregated. The Metric route uses four labeled-support statistics to select a context family without target-validation performance or query information.
Figure 4: Support-only Metric routing. Each panel shows an EEG trial and four class-separation scores from the labeled, class-balanced support subset. Routing uses no validation or query information.

Figure 5: Overall performance and context adaptation across ten datasets. Left: Ours (Metric) compared with eleven locally reproduced EEG baselines, with its numerical BAcc annotated. Right: Raw, Metric, and inspection-Oracle contexts, with numerical BAcc annotated for Raw and Oracle. Metric routing consistently improves over Raw and closely approaches the inspection Oracle. Radial positions use per-dataset min–max scaling shared across both panels.

Table 2: EEG context configurations by paradigm. For each paradigm represented by two datasets, the support-only Metric route selected the same three operators for both. Id denotes the identity operator.

Table 3: Main comparison across ten EEG datasets. The best and second-best results are shown in bold and underlined. Average ranks are computed independently on each dataset using BAcc. Without target-task fine-tuning or validation-based model selection, Ours (Metric) achieves the highest mean BAcc and the second-best average rank.
